questions.prompt: What is a Git repository?
options: The full tracked history of a project, plus its current files
A single file containing only the most recent commit
A folder that only exists on a remote server like GitHub
A backup copy made manually by a developer
questions.explain: A repository is the complete tracked history of a project — every commit ever made — together with its current working files, stored in the hidden .git folder.
questions.distractorExplain: Option C describes a common misconception: a repository exists fully on your own machine the moment you run git init or git clone — Git is distributed, so it doesn't require a remote server like GitHub to function at all.

questions.prompt: A developer creates a feature branch, and nobody else commits to main while they work. When they merge the feature branch back into main, what kind of merge does Git perform?
options: A three-way merge, creating a new merge commit
A fast-forward merge — main's pointer simply moves forward to match the feature branch
Git refuses to merge without a conflict resolution
A rebase, rewriting the feature branch's commit hashes
questions.explain: Since main never diverged while the feature branch was being worked on, Git can simply move main's pointer forward to the feature branch's latest commit — no new merge commit is needed.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about distributed version control systems like Git.
options: Every clone holds the project's complete history, not just its current files
Committing requires a live network connection to a central server
Branching is nearly instant because a branch is just a movable pointer, not a file copy
A centralized VCS like Subversion also gives every client the full history
Git can show history and diffs entirely offline
questions.explain: Distributed VCS tools like Git give every clone the complete history, so committing, branching, and browsing history all work offline. Branching is cheap specifically because a branch is a pointer, not a copy. Centralized systems like Subversion are the opposite — only the central server holds the full history, which is exactly what distributed VCS was designed to avoid.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: the area in Git where you deliberately choose which changes will go into your next commit is called the staging area, also known as the ________.
questions.explain: Git's staging area is also called "the index" — the holding area between your working directory and a committed snapshot.

questions.prompt: Match each Git term to what it actually refers to.
right: A saved snapshot of the repository at one point in time
Another copy of the repository your local repository can communicate with
The pointer tracking which branch/commit you currently have checked out
A movable pointer to a specific commit
questions.explain: HEAD tracks your current position. A branch is a movable pointer to a commit. A remote is another copy of the repository you can push to or pull from. A commit is a saved snapshot of the project at one moment.

questions.prompt: Put these steps in the correct order for tracking a new file and sharing it with a remote for the first time.
questions.explain: You first initialize the repository (git init), then stage the new file (git add), then permanently record it as a snapshot (git commit), and finally upload it to the remote (git push).

questions.prompt: Two branches both changed line 12 of the same file in different ways, and you try to merge them. What happens?
options: Git automatically picks the more recent change and merges silently
Git reports a merge conflict and pauses the merge, leaving conflict markers in the file for you to resolve
Git deletes both branches to avoid the ambiguity
Git merges successfully by keeping both lines side by side permanently
questions.explain: Git can only auto-combine non-overlapping changes. When both branches changed the exact same line differently, Git pauses the merge and inserts conflict markers for a human to resolve.

questions.prompt: What is a pull request (PR)?
options: A Git command that automatically merges two branches
A hosting-platform feature that proposes merging one branch into another, with review and automated checks built in
A type of branch protection rule
A required step before you can commit any change
questions.explain: A pull request is a feature of hosting platforms like GitHub, not Git itself — there's no git pull-request command. It wraps a proposed merge with discussion, review, and automated checks.
questions.distractorExplain: Option A is the core misconception this lesson corrects: there is no Git command that creates a pull request. Mechanically a PR still relies on ordinary branches and merges — the PR itself is a platform feature layered on top.

questions.prompt: A repository requires at least one reviewer's approval before merging. A developer with Write access opens a PR for their own change. Can they merge it themselves without anyone else's approval?
options: Yes, Write access always allows merging regardless of protection rules
No — the branch protection rule blocks the merge until the approval requirement is satisfied, regardless of their Write access
Only if they are the repository's original creator
Only if the PR has zero comments on it
questions.explain: Branch protection and repository roles work together: Write access lets you propose a change via a PR, but a required-approval rule can still block you from merging it yourself until another reviewer approves.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about effective code review, per this course.
options: A reviewer leaving only line comments, with no Approve or Request Changes, hasn't signaled whether the PR is mergeable
The main value of code review is only catching bugs a test suite would also catch
A specific, actionable comment names the real risk and suggests a concrete direction to fix it
Code review spreads shared understanding of the codebase across more than one person
Feedback on a PR should always be treated as a personal criticism of the author
questions.explain: Review's biggest value often isn't bug-catching alone — it's shared understanding and spreading conventions. A reviewer should leave an explicit Approve or Request Changes, not just scattered comments, and good comments are specific and actionable rather than vague. Feedback on code is not a personal referendum on the author, and treating it that way makes review worse for everyone.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: the PR merge strategy that combines every commit on a branch into a single new commit on the target branch is called ________ and merge.
questions.explain: Squash and merge collapses all of a feature branch's commits into one clean commit on the target branch, discarding the individual incremental commit history.

questions.prompt: Match each PR merge strategy to what it does to the target branch's history.
right: Replays the branch's commits one by one onto the target branch's tip, with no merge commit
Keeps every individual commit from the branch, plus a new merge commit
Combines all of the branch's commits into a single new commit
questions.explain: A standard merge commit preserves every individual commit and adds a merge commit. Squash and merge collapses the branch into one commit. Rebase and merge replays each commit onto the target branch's tip with no merge commit at all.

questions.prompt: Put these pull request lifecycle steps in the order they actually happen.
items: A branch with finished work is pushed to the remote
A pull request is opened, targeting main
Automated status checks run against the proposed merge
A reviewer approves or requests changes
The PR is merged and the source branch is typically deleted
questions.explain: The branch is pushed first, then a PR is opened proposing the merge, then automated checks run, then a human reviews and approves (or requests changes), and only once both checks and approval are satisfied does the PR merge.

questions.prompt: A pre-commit hook that runs a linter was never installed in a new teammate's local .git/hooks/ folder after they cloned the repository. Why not?
options: Because .git/hooks/ is not tracked by Git, so hook scripts aren't part of what a clone downloads
Because the teammate's account lacks permission to run hooks
Because hooks only work on the original author's machine
Because Git deletes all hooks automatically after 30 days
questions.explain: The .git/hooks/ folder lives inside .git, which Git itself doesn't track or version — so cloning a repo gives you only Git's unused .sample hooks, unless a team's tooling separately installs the real scripts for everyone.

questions.prompt: Why are scratch orgs well suited to a Git branch-based Salesforce workflow?
options: They are permanent, so a feature branch's org state never changes
They're disposable orgs created on demand from a tracked definition file, letting a developer test one feature branch in isolation and discard the org when done
They eliminate the need for any Apex test coverage
They automatically merge Git branches without a pull request
questions.explain: Scratch orgs are created fresh from a committed definition file, used to test a specific branch's changes in isolation, and discarded once done — avoiding the data and configuration drift a shared sandbox used by multiple developers accumulates.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about trunk-based development and feature flags.
options: Trunk-based development requires main to stay deployable at all times, backed by strong automated test coverage
A feature flag lets code merge into main continuously while staying inactive until the feature is actually ready for users
Long-lived feature branches reduce risk by deferring all integration to one large merge at the end
Trunk-based development is fundamentally incompatible with a scheduled, multi-environment release train
A feature flag decouples merging code from releasing it to users
questions.explain: Trunk-based development demands main stay deployable, which requires real test coverage. Feature flags let merged code stay inactive until ready, decoupling merge from release. Long-lived branches actually concentrate risk into one large, delayed merge rather than reducing it, and trunk-based principles can coexist with a scheduled release train — the two operate at different layers.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: the file that controls which metadata the sf CLI excludes when retrieving from or deploying to an org — separate from what Git itself tracks — is called ________.
questions.explain: .forceignore mirrors .gitignore's pattern syntax but controls a different thing entirely: what the sf CLI moves between the project and an org during retrieve/deploy, independent of Git's own tracking.

questions.prompt: Under an environment-branching strategy, match each long-lived branch to the org it typically represents.
questions.explain: Under environment branching, each long-lived branch maps one-to-one to a specific org: main to Production, uat to the UAT sandbox, qa to the QA sandbox, and develop to the integration/dev sandbox.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of a source-driven Salesforce development cycle in the correct order.
items: Create a feature branch for the work
Make the change in a scratch org or sandbox
Retrieve the metadata change into the local project with sf project retrieve start
Review the change with git status and git diff
Commit, push, and open a pull request
questions.explain: Work starts with a branch, then the actual change is made in an org, then retrieved into the local source-format project, then reviewed via git status/diff to catch any unintended metadata, and only then committed, pushed, and opened as a PR.

questions.prompt: Two branches each add a different, legitimately needed <members> entry to the same package.xml <types> block, and merging produces a conflict. What is usually the correct resolution?
options: Keep only the entry from whichever branch is merged second
Delete the entire <types> block to sidestep the conflict
Keep the union of both sides' <members> entries, removing only genuine duplicates
Regenerate package.xml from an empty manifest and start over
questions.explain: Because both sides usually added separate, legitimate components, the correct resolution is the union of both lists — not picking one side and silently discarding the other's intended addition, which is exactly the mistake that causes a component to go missing from the next deploy.
